sentences.text: Search Arena is a crowdsourced in-the-wild evaluation platform for search-augmented LLM systems based on human preference (Arena's launch post), and in the MMRS record, which carries it as a row of the MMRS meta-aggregator's census, it is the leaderboard that ranks search-enabled language models by head-to-head human votes, its unit the search-enabled model rated from those votes, its kind a leaderboard and its role evaluation (MMRS record).

Its page on arena.ai is titled 'AI Search Leaderboard: Top Models for Research' and offers overall rankings across LLMs (its card, Arena AI), one board among Arena's 'Official AI Model Rankings & Benchmarks', whose overview card ranks models in other arenas, Agent, WebDev and Image Edit among them (Arena AI).

Arena's launch post gives it two aims, to 'enable crowd-sourced evaluation of search-augmented LLMs' and to 'release a diverse, in-the-wild dataset of user–system interactions', and sets its data apart from LM-Arena's and SimpleQA's by a focus on current events and diverse real-world use cases (Arena blog).

It launched on 18 March 2025 and had collected over 11k votes across 10+ models, filtered to 7k battles, by the post of 15 April 2025, updated 2 August 2025 and first published at blog.lmarena.ai (Arena blog); Arena's leaderboard dataset dates its search data from the release on lmarena.ai on 7 August 2025 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset).

At launch it supported 11 models from Perplexity, Gemini and OpenAI, OpenAI's web search API evaluated in place of the search feature in the ChatGPT product, and its first board, on 7k votes from 18 March to 13 April, put Gemini-2.5-Pro-Grounding and Perplexity-Sonar-Reasoning-Pro at the top (Arena blog).

Its operator is Arena, formerly LMArena and Chatbot Arena, 'a public, web-based platform that evaluates large language models (LLMs)', released as Chatbot Arena on 24 April 2023, incorporated as an independent company (as LMArena) in April 2025, renamed Arena on 28 January 2026, and valued at $3.1 billion in a $200 million Series B announced on 8 October 2026 (Wikipedia); the site's footer names Arena Intelligence Inc. (Arena blog), and the MMRS record gives the operator as arena.ai on the operator's own statement and leaves the operator statement on the leaderboard page unchecked (MMRS record).

A vote is a battle: on Arena users put a prompt to two anonymous models and vote for the better response, after which the models' identities are revealed (Wikipedia), here two search-augmented answers compared, with models rated with confidence intervals from the battles (MMRS record); each response is displayed in a standardized citation format or in the provider's original one, by 'style randomization', and Arena invites model submissions and encourages public voting (Arena blog).

Scores come from a Bradley-Terry model whose coefficients are translated to the Elo scale, consistent with LM Arena (Arena blog); Arena's dataset calls the rating the 'Arena Score' and its vote_count the 'Number of battles for this model' (Arena Leaderboard Dataset); at launch Arena wrote that 'The confidence intervals are still wide, which means the leaderboard hasn’t fully settled and there’s still some uncertainty' (Arena blog).

Of the MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena studies, in which GPT-4 reached approximately 85% agreement with human preferences against approximately 81% human-human agreement, #741 states what such pairwise judgment measures: 'This is a finding about *relative* preference under specified rubrics — comparing A versus B — not about absolute quality assessment' (#741).

The systems it rates are search-augmented language models, which 'combine web search with Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve response groundedness and freshness', and whose analysis, its paper says, has rested on datasets 'limited in scale and narrow in scope, often constrained to static, single-turn, fact-checking questions' (Miroyan et al.).

Its paper, by Miroyan and ten co-authors (arXiv:2506.05334, submitted 5 June 2025, revised 2 March 2026, accepted to ICLR 2026), introduces Search Arena as 'a crowd-sourced, large-scale, human-preference dataset of over 24,000 paired multi-turn user interactions with search-augmented LLMs', spanning diverse intents and languages, with full system traces and around 12,000 human preference votes, open-sourced (Miroyan et al.); the MMRS record restates the release, over 24,000 paired multi-turn interactions with about 12,000 votes (MMRS record).
The MMRS record reads the released interactions as original outputs, preserved, on the paper's statement (MMRS record).

The paper's headline finding is that 'user preferences are influenced by the number of citations, even when the cited content does not directly support the attributed claims, uncovering a gap between perceived and actual credibility' (Miroyan et al.), which the MMRS record carries as preference rising with the number of citations even when the cited content does not support the claim it is attached to (MMRS record).

The launch post had found three features strongly correlated with preference, response length, citation count and citing YouTube and online forums or blogs; controlling for citation count gave a positive, significant coefficient (0.234, p < 0.05), only response length and citation count stayed significant under joint controls, and with the number of citations controlled the rankings converged, while standardizing citation styles had minimal effect on rankings (Arena blog).

Preference varies across cited sources: 'community-driven platforms are generally preferred and static encyclopedic sources are not always appropriate and reliable' (Miroyan et al.; restated by the MMRS record), while all models favor authoritative sources such as Wikipedia, .edu and .gov domains and OpenAI's models cite news sources for 51.3% overall (Arena blog).

Across arenas, web search does not degrade and may even improve performance in non-search settings, and quality in search settings is significantly affected when a model relies solely on its parametric knowledge (Miroyan et al.).

The MMRS record reads the board and the paper together: 'Its leaderboard rewards what users prefer, and its paper shows that preference rewarding citation count over citation support'; the paper analyses citations and the leaderboard ranks by votes, and whether the live leaderboard judges citations is left unchecked (MMRS record).

#741 names the regime of the systems it rates: 'The current moment adds a new proxy on top of the inherited stack: provenance topology in generative search', and 'The composition layer of an AI search system does not read documents and assess their substance', admitting or excluding documents on structural signals, citation neighborhoods among them, before any reading occurs (#741).

Arena publishes the board's history: its leaderboard dataset holds historical snapshots of the Arena leaderboard, a full split of all historically published leaderboards and a latest split of only the most recently published (Arena Leaderboard Dataset), released on 2 April 2026 as 'the entire history of those leaderboards' (Arena blog), its search boards published from 7 August 2025 to 13 October 2026 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset).

The latest, published 13 October 2026, ranks 42 models: gpt-5.6-sol-xhigh (openai) first at 1261.1 on 60,437 battles, qwen3.8-max (alibaba) second at 1261.1, claude-opus-4-6-search (anthropic) third at 1251.4 and ernie-5.1 (baidu) eleventh at 1226.7; with style control gpt-6.1-sol-max (openai) stands second at 1249.9 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset).

The MMRS record, which read the leaderboard page on 2026-10-28 for its counts and keeps the lifecycle apart from the observation that saw it, gives 247,944 votes across 22 models at the page's update of 25 February 2026, and the state active (MMRS record).

The Capture Registry's fetcher read the page on 2026-10-29 as updated 25 February 2026, with 22 models and 247,944 votes, Anthropic first at 1255 ± 10 and xAI second at 1225 ± 8 (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); Arena's dataset holds a snapshot of 26 February 2026 with claude-opus-4-6-search (anthropic) first at 1255.4 on 3,607 battles and grok-4.20-beta1 (xai) second at 1225.0 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset).

#1705 reads a ranking as an act: 'it compares', selects the members of a category, projects selected features onto a common field, orders them, and 'states the result as a property of the winner', so that the comparison, 'its category, its criteria, its sample and its author, has become an attribute of the thing compared'; 'A ranking's *best* is attributization in its commercial form: the ranker's act spoken in the product's voice' (#1705).

Wikipedia records that research has identified specific limitations in Arena's methodology, and that the version of Llama 4 Maverick on LMArena 'unfairly differed from the publicly available version', after which LMArena updated its policies (Wikipedia).

Of the MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena studies, in which GPT-4 reached approximately 85% agreement with human preferences against approximately 81% human-human agreement, #741 states what such pairwise judgment measures: 'This is a finding about *relative* preference under specified rubrics — comparing A versus B — not about absolute quality assessment' (#741). The systems it rates are search-augmented language models, which 'combine web search with Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve response groundedness and freshness', and whose analysis, its paper says, has rested on datasets 'limited in scale and narrow in scope, often constrained to static, single-turn, fact-checking questions' (Miroyan et al.). Its paper, by Miroyan and ten co-authors (arXiv:2506.05334, submitted 5 June 2025, revised 2 March 2026, accepted to ICLR 2026), introduces Search Arena as 'a crowd-sourced, large-scale, human-preference dataset of over 24,000 paired multi-turn user interactions with search-augmented LLMs', spanning diverse intents and languages, with full system traces and around 12,000 human preference votes, open-sourced (Miroyan et al.); the MMRS record restates the release, over 24,000 paired multi-turn interactions with about 12,000 votes (MMRS record). The MMRS record reads the released interactions as original outputs, preserved, on the paper's statement (MMRS record). The paper's headline finding is that 'user preferences are influenced by the number of citations, even when the cited content does not directly support the attributed claims, uncovering a gap between perceived and actual credibility' (Miroyan et al.), which the MMRS record carries as preference rising with the number of citations even when the cited content does not support the claim it is attached to (MMRS record). The launch post had found three features strongly correlated with preference, response length, citation count and citing YouTube and online forums or blogs; controlling for citation count gave a positive, significant coefficient (0.234, p < 0.05), only response length and citation count stayed significant under joint controls, and with the number of citations controlled the rankings converged, while standardizing citation styles had minimal effect on rankings (Arena blog). Preference varies across cited sources: 'community-driven platforms are generally preferred and static encyclopedic sources are not always appropriate and reliable' (Miroyan et al.; restated by the MMRS record), while all models favor authoritative sources such as Wikipedia, .edu and .gov domains and OpenAI's models cite news sources for 51.3% overall (Arena blog). Across arenas, web search does not degrade and may even improve performance in non-search settings, and quality in search settings is significantly affected when a model relies solely on its parametric knowledge (Miroyan et al.). The MMRS record reads the board and the paper together: 'Its leaderboard rewards what users prefer, and its paper shows that preference rewarding citation count over citation support'; the paper analyses citations and the leaderboard ranks by votes, and whether the live leaderboard judges citations is left unchecked (MMRS record). #741 names the regime of the systems it rates: 'The current moment adds a new proxy on top of the inherited stack: provenance topology in generative search', and 'The composition layer of an AI search system does not read documents and assess their substance', admitting or excluding documents on structural signals, citation neighborhoods among them, before any reading occurs (#741). Arena publishes the board's history: its leaderboard dataset holds historical snapshots of the Arena leaderboard, a full split of all historically published leaderboards and a latest split of only the most recently published (Arena Leaderboard Dataset), released on 2 April 2026 as 'the entire history of those leaderboards' (Arena blog), its search boards published from 7 August 2025 to 13 October 2026 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset). The latest, published 13 October 2026, ranks 42 models: gpt-5.6-sol-xhigh (openai) first at 1261.1 on 60,437 battles, qwen3.8-max (alibaba) second at 1261.1, claude-opus-4-6-search (anthropic) third at 1251.4 and ernie-5.1 (baidu) eleventh at 1226.7; with style control gpt-6.1-sol-max (openai) stands second at 1249.9 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset). The MMRS record, which read the leaderboard page on 2026-10-28 for its counts and keeps the lifecycle apart from the observation that saw it, gives 247,944 votes across 22 models at the page's update of 25 February 2026, and the state active (MMRS record). The Capture Registry's fetcher read the page on 2026-10-29 as updated 25 February 2026, with 22 models and 247,944 votes, Anthropic first at 1255 ± 10 and xAI second at 1225 ± 8 (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); Arena's dataset holds a snapshot of 26 February 2026 with claude-opus-4-6-search (anthropic) first at 1255.4 on 3,607 battles and grok-4.20-beta1 (xai) second at 1225.0 (Arena Leaderboard Dataset). #1705 reads a ranking as an act: 'it compares', selects the members of a category, projects selected features onto a common field, orders them, and 'states the result as a property of the winner', so that the comparison, 'its category, its criteria, its sample and its author, has become an attribute of the thing compared'; 'A ranking's *best* is attributization in its commercial form: the ranker's act spoken in the product's voice' (#1705). Wikipedia records that research has identified specific limitations in Arena's methodology, and that the version of Llama 4 Maverick on LMArena 'unfairly differed from the publicly available version', after which LMArena updated its policies (Wikipedia). Asked 'search arena leaderboard' on 29 October 2026, Google's AI Overview, on the registry's innocent reading, gave 'the top models and their ratings, with links to the boards'; the Capture Registry records 'No operator, no method (head-to-head human votes), no counts, and none of the dataset paper's findings on citation; the composition is a table', the Overview returning 'rankings and no account of the leaderboard' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). Against the page as read, 'The composed table's ratings, providers and order do not match it', and the registry, having checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages, leaves open which page is current: 'Google may hold a later render' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The MMRS record, each of whose assertions carries a source and a basis, links that capture as 'the composition layer's account of the entity, seated in the Capture Registry', and reads admission to the board as not requiring harm (MMRS record). Wikipedia has no article at 'Search Arena', and its article on the operator, to which 'LMArena' and 'Chatbot Arena' redirect, does not name it (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29); of the entity and its composition the Capture Registry says 'The record keeps the entity; the capture keeps what was composed in its place' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

E_F.definition: Search Arena, a crowdsourced in-the-wild evaluation platform for search-augmented LLM systems based on human preference (B3), launched 18 March 2025 by Arena (formerly LMArena and Chatbot Arena, Arena Intelligence Inc.; B8, B3), its page the 'AI Search Leaderboard: Top Models for Research' (B1); users vote between two anonymous answers, scores from a Bradley-Terry model on the Elo scale (B3, B8), the 'Arena Score' (B5); its paper (Miroyan et al., arXiv:2506.05334, ICLR 2026) a crowd-sourced human-preference dataset of over 24,000 paired interactions with about 12,000 votes, finding that preference follows the number of citations even when the cited content does not support the claims (B4); its published boards from 7 August 2025, the latest of 13 October 2026 ranking 42 models (B5, B6). No Wikipedia article (B7); the operator's article does not name it (B8).

E_A.definition: Search Arena as the MMRS meta-aggregator records it (editor Lee Sharks, 2026-10-28, corrected 2026-10-29), a row of its census: the leaderboard on arena.ai that ranks search-enabled language models by head-to-head human votes, its unit the search-enabled model rated from those votes, its kind a leaderboard and its role evaluation, its operator arena.ai on the operator's statement; 247,944 votes across 22 models at the page's update of 25 February 2026, as read on 2026-10-28, active; its dataset paper's interactions preserved as original outputs; a board that rewards what users prefer, where that preference rewards citation count over citation support, whether the live board judges citations unchecked; and, at the Capture Registry's address 'search arena leaderboard' (2026-10-29), an entity whose composition is a table in its place. Pairwise judgment of the kind it aggregates measures relative preference, not absolute quality (#741); the systems it rates admit documents on structural signals before reading (#741); a ranking states its comparison as the winner's attribute (#1705).
